paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by complete deficiency of tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2). Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that its core clinical phenotype is mycobacterial and/or viral infections, caused by impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta. They also concluded that impaired IL-6 responses and hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency in humans. Wu et al. (2020) summarized the disorder as autosomal recessive and marked by normal lymphocyte counts with defects in signaling by multiple cytokines. Patients are susceptible to viruses or intracellular bacteria, and serum IgE may or may not be elevated.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy with TYK2 deficiency born to healthy first-cousin parents. He received BCG vaccine at 2 months and developed left axillary lymphadenopathy at 8 months. By 21 months this had progressed to disseminated BCG disease with fistulous cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenitis. M. bovis BCG was isolated, and he responded to antimycobacterial treatment. At age 8 years he developed neurobrucellosis, with Brucella in blood and CSF cultures. This left him with severe hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was cured with acyclovir. The patient had none of the cardinal features of hyper-IgE syndrome: he had no skeletal or dental abnormalities, no coarse facies, no atopy or asthma, and no skin problems such as candidiasis, boils, folliculitis, or cold abscess. He also had no staphylococcal infections. The authors noted that this contrasted with the previously reported Japanese patient with TYK2 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) described 7 TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 unrelated families from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. All had mycobacterial and/or viral infections but none of the features of HIES. In particular, they did not have atopy, high serum IgE, or staphylococcal disease, and none had documented pyogenic or fungal infections, including mucocutaneous candidiasis. All had been BCG vaccinated. Patients P1 through P5 had normal numbers of central and effector memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, unlike patients with autosomal dominant HIES. The authors suggested that reactivation of chronic viral infections results from impaired IFN-alpha/beta responses rather than from a memory T-cell defect.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy with BCG disease, born in 2016 to young nonconsanguineous parents. After BCG vaccination on day 3 of life, he had repeated abscess and ulceration at the injection site, which had healed by 10 months. At 14 months he developed BCG-associated left axillary lymph node tuberculosis without lung involvement; acid-fast bacilli and Mycobacterium bovis BCG were isolated from the draining sinuses. From 6 months of age he had recurrent respiratory tract infections, with pneumonia or upper respiratory infection every 1 to 2 months, as well as diarrhea. Pathogens found included Salmonella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and BCG, and IgM serology was positive for influenza A and B. He had no significant viral or fungal infections and no high serum IgE, atopy, staphylococcal disease, or lymphopenia. He also had a small head circumference and delayed speech, saying his first simple words at 3 years 4 months, but his motor development was normal.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) also showed that TYK2-deficient cells had impaired, but not abolished, responses to IFN-alpha/beta. STAT1 phosphorylation was reduced and STAT3 phosphorylation was absent, and both were restored by wildtype TYK2. The cells also showed reduced GAF and ISGF3 DNA binding and low basal ISG expression. IFN-alpha failed to control VSV replication in EBV-B and HVS-T cells and only partly controlled it in fibroblasts. The authors suggested that these defects account for the viral infections and their mild course, similar to partial STAT1 deficiency. TYK2-deficient cells responded normally to IFN-lambda-1 and IFN-lambda-3 in terms of IFIT1 induction, although basal IFIT1 mRNA was extremely low. Responses to IL-27, IFN-gamma, IL-21, and LIF were normal, indicating that TYK2 is redundant for these pathways. All TYK2-deficient patients had impaired, but not abolished, responses to IL-10. STAT3 phosphorylation was reduced and was rescued by wildtype TYK2, SOCS3 induction was impaired, and suppression of LPS-induced TNF in P2 macrophages was intermediate. The residual IL-10 responses probably account for the lack of early-onset colitis. Because P1, who was atopic, and the other, nonatopic patients had equally impaired IL-10 responses, the authors considered IL-10 defects unlikely to cause HIES.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated Turkish children with COVID-19 pneumonia, each born to consanguineous parents, Zhang et al. (2022) identified the same homozygous frameshift mutation in the TYK2 gene (P216Rfs*14). The mutation was found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and family segregation analysis confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance. The 3-year-old younger sister of one patient was also homozygous for the mutation. She had critical influenza pneumonia and disseminated varicella but had not been infected with SARS-CoV-2. The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression in patient cells, and the authors confirmed that it was loss-of-function. SARS-CoV-2-infected fibroblasts from a patient homozygous for P216fs*14 did not control viral replication normally. These cells also failed to induce ISGs after infection or after IFN-alpha-2b pretreatment.
